column2: Back
IDS detects and alerts out of band; IPS detects and blocks inline in the path.

#separator:: NIDS vs HIDS — what does each see?
column2: NIDS = packets on a network segment (needs tap/SPAN); HIDS = local logs, file integrity, and syscalls on one host.

#separator:: Why is a signature NIDS blind to encrypted C2?
column2: It can only see ciphertext; content signatures need readable payload. Anomaly/flow analysis still catches the behavioral shape.
Signature = match known-bad patterns (blind to 0-day); anomaly = deviation from a learned baseline (catches unknowns, more false positives).

#separator:: Which alert outcome is the dangerous one?
column2: False negative — a real attack that is missed (no alert).

#separator:: Insertion attack on an IDS — who accepts the packet?
column2: The IDS accepts it; the end host rejects it. Pads the IDS view so the signature never matches.

#separator:: Evasion attack on an IDS — who accepts the packet?
column2: The end host accepts it; the IDS rejects or misses it. Attack reaches the target but skips IDS reassembly.

#separator:: Third Ptacek & Newsham category besides insertion/evasion?
column2: Denial of service — exhaust, blind, or fail-open the IDS.

#separator:: Packet-filter firewall — OSI layer and decision basis?
column2: Layer 3–4; stateless ACLs on IP, port, protocol, and flags — no session memory.

#separator:: Stateful inspection firewall — what does it add?
column2: A connection state table, so it allows the return traffic of established flows.
Layer 7 — inspects full payload, terminates and re-originates the connection; deep but slow.
A firewall combining Layer 3–7 controls: App-ID, user identity, integrated IPS, and TLS inspection (DPI).

#separator:: What is a DMZ / screened subnet?
column2: A buffer zone for internet-facing services between an outer and inner firewall, so a compromise there can't reach the internal LAN.
A hardened, exposed host (jump/proxy) built to withstand attack; minimal services, heavy logging.
Fragment packets: -f ≈ 8-byte fragments, -ff ≈ 16-byte, to break payload signatures.
The value must be a multiple of 8 (8, 16, 24…); -f ≈ MTU 8, -ff ≈ MTU 16.
Decoys: spray spoofed source IPs (e.g. -D RND:5 or ip1,ME,ip2) so the real scanner hides in the crowd.
Spoof the source port (e.g. 53/80/443) to slip past ACLs that trust a 'safe' port.
Append N random bytes to each packet to break length-based signatures.
Sends a bad TCP/UDP checksum; the end host drops it (insertion concept) while it can fingerprint filtering devices.
Spoof the source MAC (0 = random) to hide the Layer-2 origin.
-T0 paranoid, -T1 sneaky … -T5 insane; low values slow the scan to dodge rate-based alerts.

#separator:: DNS tunneling — tell-tale signal and tools?
column2: High volume of long, high-entropy TXT/A queries to one domain; tools: iodine, dnscat2.
Hide payload in echo request/reply data; tools: Loki, ptunnel.
Low = emulated services (safer, less data); high = real OS/services (richer data, more risk).
Production = early-warning tripwire inside your net; research = study attacker TTPs in depth.

#separator:: How does an attacker fingerprint a honeypot?
column2: Canned banners, too-consistent open services, abnormal latency/tarpit stalling, VM/sandbox artifacts, no real user activity.
Sniffer, packet logger, and NIDS (signature IDS/IPS).
Multi-threaded, Snort-rule compatible, emits EVE JSON (read alerts with jq on eve.json).

#separator:: PAM angle: which control catches evasion that fools network IDS?
column2: PTA (Privileged Threat Analytics) — behavioral/UEBA on the identity plane (Golden Ticket, DCSync, PtH).

#separator:: PAM angle: why does log tampering fail against the Vault?
column2: The Digital Vault audit is tamper-evident and append-only, so it survives the anti-forensics evasion relies on.

#separator:: PAM egress control for jump/bastion hosts?
column2: Default-deny egress so a foothold can't tunnel out over DNS/HTTP/ICMP; alert when a log source goes silent.
